JSON: Name: agentarceval_pipeline Title: AgentArcEval: a scenario-based architecture evaluation pipeline for foundation-model-based agents addressing goal-directed autonomy, guardrail modeling, and continuous runtime assessment Short Hypothesis: Applying a scenario-based architecture evaluation pipeline that integrates agent-specific general scenarios, explicit guardrail modeling, and continuous runtime monitoring increases the true positive detection rate of architecture-level risks in foundation-model-based agents by at least 20 percentage points compared to evaluations using standard ATAM or CBAM procedures. Related Work: Existing architecture-evaluation approaches are primarily design-time and scenario-driven (e.g., tradeoff and cost–benefit frameworks) or focused on runtime adaptation and self-adaptive decisioning. Traditional methods handle epistemic uncertainty well but provide limited support for continuous aleatory uncertainty arising during runtime operation. Cost–benefit extensions add economic assessment but do not capture agent-specific concerns such as goal decomposition, dynamic requirement generation, or multi-layered guardrails. Runtime evaluation work addresses monitoring and some automated tradeoff management but typically lacks structured scenario catalogues and explicit modeling of guardrails that allow agents to autonomously make requirement-level tradeoffs. Prior agent-oriented reference architectures describe modular components (context engineering, memory, reasoning, workflow execution, tool selection) but do not include a validated evaluation pipeline combining design-time scenario elicitation, prioritization, and runtime reassessment tailored to FM-based agent behaviors. Limitations therefore include insufficient handling of goal-directed autonomy, absence of agent-specific scenario catalogues, weak support for guardrail specification as an architectural control point, and lack of empirical comparisons against classical evaluation methods in real-world agents. Abstract: Evaluating architectures of foundation-model-based agents requires new methods because agents combine opaque foundation models with external components, make autonomous requirement-level trade-offs, and evolve continuously. We introduce a structured research pipeline operationalizing AgentArcEval: a scenario-based evaluation method that integrates an agent-specific catalogue of general scenarios, explicit guardrail modeling, and continuous runtime assessment to surface architecture-level risks and trade-offs early and during operation. The pipeline prescribes inputs (project spec, architecture spec, governance constraints, runtime data), a workshop-driven scenario definition and prioritization step, mapping of scenarios to architectural artifacts, and iterative design-time and runtime analyses that produce prioritized risk lists and prescriptive recommendations. The main contribution is a reproducible experimental protocol and benchmark suite for comparing AgentArcEval against standard architecture-evaluation methods. Expected outcomes are quantified improvements in detection of architecture-level vulnerabilities, better coverage of agent-specific failure modes, and measurable insights into trade-offs between accuracy, safety, observability, and efficiency for FM-based agents. Experiments: Datasets and systems: (1) Real-world deployed agents: Luna tax copilot (proprietary), two additional production FM-based agent deployments (proprietary, N=2); (2) Open-source agent repositories (N=6) representing diverse design patterns; (3) Synthetic benchmark agents (N=5) created by composing standard components (context engine, retriever, vector DB, workflows, guardrails) with controlled fault injections. Total agents evaluated: 14. Scenario suite: the provided catalogue of 11 general scenarios expanded to 60 context-specific scenarios per agent via the defined workshop protocol. Ground truth: for each synthetic agent and for a subset of open-source agents, inject labeled architecture-level faults (categories: retrieval failure, guardrail bypass, memory corruption, workflow deadlock, tool compromise) with known timestamps; for proprietary agents use post-hoc domain-expert annotations for observed failures. Baselines: (A) ATAM adapted to FM systems, (B) CBAM adapted to FM systems, (C) runtime-only monitoring baseline (logs + alarms without scenario-driven design), (D) automated static checklist baseline. Evaluation metrics: true positive detection rate (TPR) of architecture-level faults, precision, recall, F1, time-to-detection for runtime faults (seconds/minutes), scenario coverage percentage, false positive rate, evaluator effort (person-hours), and recommendation actionability score (binary label per recommendation). Experimental setup: randomized crossover trial with 12 architecture evaluators (experienced architects); each evaluator performs three assigned methods per agent under a 6-hour time budget, counterbalanced to remove ordering effects. Automated components of AgentArcEval (scenario instantiation, mapping to artifacts) are provided as scripts; ATAM/CBAM follow standard documented procedures. Repeats and statistics: each evaluator–agent–method cell repeated with three seeded runs for stochastic components (total runs ≥1,512). Statistical analysis: paired comparisons of TPR and time-to-detection using paired t-test and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals; perform ablation studies: (i) AgentArcEval without scenario catalogue (random scenarios), (ii) AgentArcEval without guardrail modeling, (iii) AgentArcEval without continuous runtime monitoring. Report effect sizes and significance for each ablation relative to full pipeline. Risk Factors and Limitations: Subjectivity and stakeholder dependence: scenario elicitation and prioritization rely on human judgment, producing variability across evaluators. Ground-truth labeling: definitive labels for architecture-level faults in real deployed agents may be unavailable or noisy, limiting validity of detection metrics. Coverage bias: selected agents and injected faults may not represent the full diversity of FM-based agent designs or real-world failure modes. Scalability: the workshop-driven scenario generation and manual analysis steps may not scale to very large fleets of agents or frequent evaluation cycles. Compute and cost constraints: reranking, repeated LLM-based assessments, and runtime monitoring of high-throughput agents entail nontrivial compute and operational expense. Temporal drift: foundation model updates and external tool changes can invalidate prior evaluations and ground truth, complicating longitudinal assessment. Masking and false negatives: guardrails and runtime mitigations can mask latent architecture faults, reducing detectability. Regulatory and data constraints: access to production logs or proprietary legal corpora may be restricted, limiting reproducibility. Generalization limits: the pipeline tuned on tax and similar transactional domains may not transfer directly to embodied, real-time, or safety-critical agent domains without adaptation.
